sample_unit: aesthetic surgery procedures (discharge instruction outputs per tool)

links.outcome: Reading grade level and reading ease of LLM-generated patient discharge instructions
links.effect: Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level 9.3 ± 1.0 (OpenEvidence) vs 9.2 ± 0.6 (ChatGPT-5); Reading Ease 40.0 ± 6.6 vs 41.0 5.5, i.e., difficult-to-read material for both tools.
links.quote: as well as on the Flesch Kincaid Grade Level (9.3 ± 1.0 vs 9.2 ± 0.6, P = .8) and the Flesch Reading Ease Score (40.0 ± 6.6 vs 41.0 ± 5.5, P = .6).

links.outcome: Citation accuracy of sources in generative AI patient education outputs
links.effect: Citation accuracy (1-4 Likert) was 2.4 ± 1.3 for OpenEvidence vs 1.5 ± 0.7 for ChatGPT-5 (P = .007); both imperfect, ChatGPT-5 notably poor.
links.quote: OpenEvidence scored significantly higher than ChatGPT-5 in DISCERN (3.3 ± 0.4 vs 1.7 ± 0.4, P < .001) and the citation accuracy scale (2.4 ± 1.3 vs 1.5 ± 0.7, P = .007).

links.outcome: Quality and citation accuracy of evidence-grounded (OpenEvidence) vs general LLM outputs
links.effect: OpenEvidence, trained on peer-reviewed literature, had higher DISCERN quality (3.3 vs 1.7, P < .001) and citation accuracy (2.4 vs 1.5, P = .007) than ChatGPT-5.
links.quote: OpenEvidence generated materials of significantly higher quality and reliability than ChatGPT, suggesting it may serve as a more reliable alternative for patient education in aesthetic surgery practice.

screen.reason: The study empirically evaluates and compares the output quality, readability, and citation accuracy of two LLMs (ChatGPT and OpenEvidence) for generating patient education materials, but it does not test a deployment practice or safeguard.
